resources.string: Fire and hazmat weather for a point on the map, kept when the network drops
The last-3-days switch applies to the list too. Near me, on the map, by state or region: swipe on to the Spot forecasts page.
Show spot forecasts on the map?
Atmosphere will ask the National Weather Service for the open spot forecast requests and draw them on the map. Your position is not sent. Server: mapservices.weather.noaa.gov
Here: outside the area being drawn
Show or hide this storm\'s maps
Hurricanes from the National Hurricane Center (%1$s)
Atmosphere will ask the National Hurricane Center which storms are running, and draw their forecast cones and tracks on the map. Your position is not sent. Server: mapservices.weather.noaa.gov
Show or hide this layer\'s settings
Radar from the US National Weather Service (%1$s)

Wind comes from the US National Weather Service, drawn as moving air over the map.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere ask them for wind over the part of the map you are looking at. Nothing else about you is sent.

Server: nomads.ncep.noaa.gov
Drawn for the middle of the map. Zoom in to see all of it.

Smoke comes from the US National Weather Service's forecast model, the same one the wind comes from: where the smoke is and how thick, near the ground or through the whole sky.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere ask them for smoke over the part of the map you are looking at. Nothing else about you is sent.

Server: nomads.ncep.noaa.gov
Here: outside the areas EPA has drawn
Air quality from the U.S. EPA\'s AirNow (%1$s)

Air quality comes from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's AirNow: the latest hour of ozone and fine particles, measured at monitors and drawn in the six Air Quality Index colors.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere ask EPA for the map of the whole country. Your position is not sent.

Server: services.arcgis.com
Warnings from the US National Weather Service (%1$s)

Warnings come from the US National Weather Service: Red Flag Warnings, Fire Weather Watches and every other warning and watch in effect, drawn in the Weather Service's own colors.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere download the country's active warnings and the shapes of the areas they cover. Your position is not sent.

Server: api.weather.gov
Every spot forecast request the National Weather Service has open, with the forecast they issued for each. Narrow it to near you, the map, a state or a region.
The National Weather Service takes spot requests on their own form and it cannot be filled in from here. Copy the point, open the form, then hold its USNG box, paste, and press Plot USNG.
Tap the map where the forecast is for

What you type goes to the US Census Bureau first, which answers with the street address or with nothing. If it has no answer, %1$s is asked \u2014 the address finder picked in ATAK\'s settings, which is also sent the area of the map on screen. You get to see what came back before it is used.
Copied %1$s \u2014 on the form, paste it into the USNG box and press Plot USNG
ATAK has no address search set up

Spot forecasts from the US National Weather Service (mapservices.weather.noaa.gov, api.weather.gov). Address search uses the US Census Bureau (geocoding.geo.census.gov), then the geocoder ATAK is set to.

Spot forecasts come from the US National Weather Service: the open requests from their spot forecast map service, and each forecast from their weather API.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere download the whole country's list and filter it on this phone. Your position is not sent.

Servers: mapservices.weather.noaa.gov, api.weather.gov

Radar comes from the US National Weather Service, the same picture their own radar site draws.

Turning it on lets Atmosphere ask them for radar over the part of the map you are looking at. Nothing else about you is sent.

Server: opengeo.ncep.noaa.gov
